site.name: meadowos
site.summary: meadowos-clone Fictional self-hosted home OS "MeadowOS" marketing site (magazine / zine-style long-scroll narrative). Pages | File | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `index.html` | Single-page long scroll: thin top nav + progress bar; hero with hand-drawn SVG house and flower illustration; five chapters (Roman numerals I–V) of magazine-prose with pull quotes and chapter illustrations; mid-page "Garden" 6-card plant-app grid (Nextfile / Bramble / Cottage / Smithy / Hearth / Postcard); reviewer quotes; terminal-style .iso download block + platform pills + minimum / recommended specs; six numbered manifesto items; dark footer | | `styles.css` | Brand color #2F5233 dark green, accent terracotta + wheat yellow, cream paper background; Crimson Pro serif + Inter; cards with slight rotate + paper-shadow; responsive | | `script.js` | Top scroll progress bar; smooth anchor scrolling; clicking "Download .iso" triggers a fake download-progress modal (increments to 100% then shows SHA256 verification passed) |

run_plan.goal: Exhaustively explore the single-page MeadowOS landing experience, validating the long-scroll narrative, anchor-based navigation, Garden/docs/download sections, and the fake download modal across desktop and mobile viewports.
run_plan.summary: The run should focus on the core landing-page journey from hero to download, since the prescan shows only one HTML page with in-page anchors rather than separate adjacent pages. Start by validating top-nav anchor behavior and long-scroll readability, then inspect the Garden app grid, docs/download section, and the modal-driven download interaction in depth. Because mobile is in scope and the prescan already flags small tap targets, repeat critical navigation and CTA checks on a mobile viewport and look for sticky-nav, anchor, and modal usability issues.
assumptions: There is only one explorable HTML page (index.html); 'Story', 'Garden', 'Docs', and 'Get the .iso' are in-page anchor links, not separate pages.
The primary interactive state beyond scrolling/navigation is the fake download-progress modal triggered by the download button.
Footer links such as 'GitHub' and 'Matrix room' may be placeholders because their hrefs are '#', so they should be checked for behavior but not assumed to lead to real destinations.
The visible 'Read time · ~6 min' and scroll progress bar are part of the intended editorial long-scroll experience and should be assessed during scrolling.
risk_hotspots: Top navigation anchor links (Story/Garden/Docs/Get the .iso): smooth-scroll accuracy, active context, and potential header overlap on anchored sections.
Scroll progress bar on index.html: correctness as the user moves through a very long page.
Long-scroll narrative chapters I–V: readability, pacing, and whether section transitions remain clear over the full page length.
Garden 6-card app grid (Nextfile, Bramble, Cottage, Smithy, Hearth, Postcard): card layout consistency and whether cards appear interactive or purely informational.
Download button 'Download · meadowos-0.7.iso · 1.2 GB': modal launch reliability and CTA clarity.
Fake download-progress modal: progress increments, completion to 100%, 'SHA256 verification passed' end state, dismiss/recovery behavior, and any blocking/focus issues.
Footer placeholder links (GitHub, Matrix room): potential dead-end behavior and expectation mismatch.
Mobile nav/footer tap targets: prescan already identified multiple controls below recommended mobile target sizes.

phases.title: Desktop first-pass orientation and anchor flow
phases.objective: Validate the main landing-page path from hero through anchored sections using the top navigation and natural scrolling.
key_checks: Confirm the hero presents the product proposition clearly before scrolling.
Click Story, Garden, Docs, and Get the .iso from the top nav and verify each scrolls to the intended section.
Check whether anchored sections are fully visible after navigation and not hidden beneath the top nav.
Observe whether smooth scrolling feels controlled and whether the URL/hash behavior is sensible for a single-page site.
Scroll manually through the page to compare anchor jumps with the natural reading flow.
exit_criteria: All four visible top-nav links have been exercised at least once.
Each anchor target is located and confirmed to map to the expected section content.
Any header-overlap, disorientation, or anchor mismatch issues are documented.

phases.title: Narrative content and long-scroll behavior
phases.objective: Assess the editorial long-form experience, including chapter structure, progress feedback, and readability over the full page.
key_checks: Read/skim through the chapter sequence I–V and verify section headings and pull-quote moments remain discoverable.
Monitor the scroll progress bar from top to bottom for accuracy and smoothness.
Check whether the 'Read time · ~6 min' framing feels consistent with page length and pacing.
Inspect transitions between hero, story chapters, Garden, reviewer quotes, download/specs, manifesto items, and footer for narrative coherence.
Note any fatigue points such as overly dense text blocks, weak section separation, or confusing shifts in tone/content.
exit_criteria: Top, middle, and bottom page regions have all been reviewed in sequence.
Progress bar behavior has been observed during substantial scrolling.
Long-scroll UX strengths and breakdowns are captured with section-specific evidence.

phases.title: Garden, docs, and footer affordance validation
phases.objective: Examine the secondary content clusters that support the primary story: the Garden app grid, docs/specs area, and footer links.
key_checks: Inspect all six Garden cards (Nextfile, Bramble, Cottage, Smithy, Hearth, Postcard) for consistency in presentation and affordance.
Determine whether Garden cards look clickable or static, and verify actual behavior where possible.
Review the docs/download section for clarity of the .iso offering, platform pills, and minimum/recommended specs presentation mentioned in the prescan summary.
Check whether the docs anchor lands at the expected installation/specification area.
Test footer links GitHub and Matrix room to confirm whether they are functional links or placeholders.
exit_criteria: All six Garden items have been visually reviewed.
Docs/specs/download support content has been inspected for clarity.
Footer link behavior is confirmed and any dead-end behavior is recorded.

phases.title: Download modal and recovery states
phases.objective: Deeply validate the most stateful interaction on the site: the fake .iso download modal and its completion flow.
key_checks: Trigger the download using the main download button and confirm the modal opens reliably.
Observe progress updates from initial state through 100% completion.
Verify the terminal-style completion message includes the reported 'SHA256 verification passed' state.
Check whether the modal can be dismissed/closed at different points if controls are available.
Assess whether background scrolling or interaction is blocked appropriately while the modal is open.
After closing or finishing, confirm the page returns to a usable state without losing context.
exit_criteria: The download modal has been run through to completion at least once.
Any available close/dismiss/retry path has been exercised.
Blocking, focus, or recovery issues for the modal interaction are documented.

phases.title: Mobile critical-path verification
phases.objective: Repeat the highest-value checks on mobile, emphasizing tap target usability, section navigation, long-scroll legibility, and modal behavior.
key_checks: Re-test Story, Garden, Docs, and Get the .iso on a mobile viewport for tap reliability and anchor accuracy.
Validate whether the top nav remains usable on mobile and whether any controls are cramped, wrapped, or obscured.
Pay special attention to prescan-reported small tap targets in nav and footer.
Confirm the Garden cards and download area remain readable and well spaced on smaller screens.
Re-run the download modal on mobile and check for viewport fit, clipping, and dismissibility.
Test footer links on mobile to see whether small target sizes make them error-prone.
exit_criteria: Critical nav and CTA interactions have been repeated on mobile.
At least one complete top-to-download journey has been exercised on mobile.
Mobile-specific issues around tap size, layout density, or modal fit are captured.

coverage_targets.pages: Visit the only known HTML page, index.html, and cover all major in-page sections from hero through footer.
coverage_targets.features: Exercise all visible top-nav anchors, inspect the six Garden cards, review the docs/specs/download content, test footer links, and run the download modal through its full progress/completion flow.
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat the navigation, long-scroll, download CTA, modal, and footer-link checks on a mobile viewport, with special focus on the small tap-target warnings already seen in prescan.

notes: Do not spend time searching for additional pages unless the live run reveals undisclosed navigation; prescan only shows index.html.
Prioritize interaction evidence over visual nitpicks: the standout custom behaviors are smooth anchor scrolling, scroll progress, and the fake terminal-style download modal.
If a control has no meaningful behavior (for example placeholder footer links), record expectation mismatch rather than forcing deeper exploration.

prescan_summary.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
prescan_summary.visible_text_excerpt: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because th

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t
